claim: The demonstrated duplicate-key INSERT error (1062, without IGNORE) rolls back that statement; the earlier and later INSERTs commit in the same InnoDB transaction. This does not describe deadlock or connection errors.
On InnoDB, the demonstrated CHECK error leaves bob's earlier credit in A's transaction; explicit ROLLBACK then discards both balances' changes.

With autocommit=1 on InnoDB, A's successful standalone UPDATE is visible to B's later standalone SELECT. B excludes A's explicit-transaction UPDATE until COMMIT; a pre-existing REPEATABLE READ snapshot need not refresh.
Rolling back to an outer savepoint discards inner savepoints along with their work; RELEASE keeps the changes but forfeits the rollback point.
In this InnoDB INSERT branch, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT removes the successful branch INSERT after a 1062 error, preserves the earlier INSERT, and allows the replacement branch to commit.

At READ UNCOMMITTED two concurrent transactions can each read the other's uncommitted write (Adya's G1c, "circular information flow"); an exchange no serial order can explain. The repeated READ COMMITTED schedule excludes those dirty cross-reads, but its two old reads do not prove serializability.

In this InnoDB REPEATABLE READ schedule, A's UPDATE computes from B's committed 150, not its snapshot's 100, and A reads its own result 200. In the second attempt A waits for B's commit of 300 and produces 350.

At READ UNCOMMITTED, MySQL serves other transactions' uncommitted changes including the asserted 999 that A later rolls back. The value existed uncommitted, but never became part of committed history.

In this InnoDB READ UNCOMMITTED schedule, B's UPDATE of A's uncommitted row waits until A commits. Both of B's later prices are asserted after B commits. All-level dirty-write exclusion needs the row-lock contract.

At READ UNCOMMITTED a reader can observe an intermediate value the writer later overwrites before committing (Adya's G1b, "intermediate read"); a number absent from committed history. In the repeated READ COMMITTED schedule, B reads 110 while A's draft 555 is uncommitted.
Two read-modify-write transactions at READ COMMITTED can silently overwrite each other: two deposits of 10 grow the balance by only 10.

In this InnoDB REPEATABLE READ schedule, both transactions read 100 and commit writes of that value plus 10 without error; the final balance is 110, not 120. A stale literal write is not rejected merely for staleness.
At READ COMMITTED, a transaction can read two different values for the same row; other transactions' commits become visible between its statements.

At READ UNCOMMITTED a reader can see a later transaction's uncommitted overwrite of one row while relying on the overwritten transaction's other row (Adya's OTV, "observed transaction vanishes"); the committed transaction is visible only in pieces in this schedule. The repeated READ COMMITTED SELECTs exclude A's draft and see both rows after commit; separate statements do not have one shared snapshot.
At READ COMMITTED, re-running the same range query inside one transaction can return rows that weren't there before; phantoms.

At READ COMMITTED, a transaction reading two rows around a concurrent transfer observes money that never existed (Adya's G-single, "read skew"); the repeated REPEATABLE READ schedule returns 25 and 75 from one snapshot, with no writes by the reader.

In this InnoDB REPEATABLE READ schedule, the first consistent SELECT includes a commit after BEGIN. Later consistent SELECTs exclude B's later UPDATE and INSERT, include A's own UPDATE, and refresh after A commits.
An UPDATE at READ COMMITTED that waited for a lock re-evaluates its WHERE clause against the new row version; rows that no longer match are silently skipped.

In this InnoDB REPEATABLE READ schedule, A's DELETE of balance=20 finds no current matching row after B commits 15/25, while A's consistent SELECT still returns snapshot balance 20. The DELETE affects zero rows.
Two REPEATABLE READ transactions can each validate an invariant against their snapshots, write to different rows, and both commit; leaving the invariant broken. This is write skew.

In these explicit InnoDB SERIALIZABLE transactions with deadlock detection enabled, the count SELECTs take shared locks. This schedule rejects B's UPDATE with 1213, A commits, and a fresh B attempt sees one doctor and declines to leave. Other schedules need not select B as victim.
An ALTER TABLE queued behind one long transaction blocks every later query on that table — even plain SELECTs — because they must queue behind its exclusive metadata-lock request.
With lock_wait_timeout set, a migration that can't get its metadata lock fails fast (errno 1205) instead of queueing — and other sessions' queries are never blocked behind it.
The same two opposite-direction transfers cannot deadlock if both transactions lock the rows in the same (id) order first — the second simply waits its turn.
Two transactions locking the same rows in opposite order deadlock; InnoDB detects the cycle instantly and rolls back one of them with errno 1213 so the other can finish.

INSERTing a child row locks the referenced parent row with a plain shared lock: even a non-key UPDATE of the parent blocks until the child commits (PostgreSQL's FOR KEY SHARE would allow it), and deleting a referenced parent fails outright.
A row locked with SELECT FOR UPDATE can still be read by everyone, but any write to it waits until the locking transaction ends.

Under REPEATABLE READ a locking read on a range takes next-key locks — the matching rows AND the gaps between them — so INSERTs into the range block until the reader finishes. Under READ COMMITTED only the found rows are locked and the same INSERT sails through.
InnoDB row locks come in exactly two strengths — S locks coexist with each other but block writers, X locks block everything. There is no PostgreSQL-style four-mode ladder.
Sessions waiting for the same row lock pile up behind the holder, visible live in sys.innodb_lock_waits — and every queued update lands once the holder commits.
With innodb_lock_wait_timeout set, a statement waits for a row lock only that long, then fails with errno 1205 — only the statement is rolled back, the transaction survives.

data_locks shows every lock a transaction holds — a single-row UPDATE takes an intention lock on the table plus a record lock on the row — and a waiter shows up as WAITING, findable via sys.innodb_lock_waits.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT refuses to wait: if the row is locked it fails immediately with errno 3572 instead of joining the lock queue.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED silently skips locked rows, so concurrent workers each grab a different row without ever waiting — the backbone of SQL job queues.

While any read view stays open, purge cannot remove the undo history behind it: every committed write transaction adds to the history list, and the history list length — InnoDB's bloat metric — grows for as long as the reader lives.

BEGIN does not take the snapshot — the transaction's first read does. START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT takes it immediately. And until it writes, a transaction doesn't even get a real transaction ID — readers are cheap by design.

A committed DELETE removes rows only from the current version of the table. A transaction whose read view predates it keeps reading the old versions, rebuilt on demand from the undo log — long after the "real" rows are gone.

GET_LOCK serializes application-defined work with no table involved: timeout 0 gives an instant yes/no, a positive timeout gives a bounded wait, and the lock ignores transactions entirely — only RELEASE_LOCK (or disconnecting) lets go.
"SELECT first, INSERT if absent" cannot enforce uniqueness: two concurrent requests both see 0 rows, both insert, and the duplicate lands without any error.
UPDATE ... SET balance = balance + 10 reads and writes in one statement: the second writer waits for the first and stacks on top — both deposits survive, at any isolation level.

When the new value must be computed in application code, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE serializes the read-modify-write: the second reader waits and then reads the committed 110 — a locking read pierces the snapshot by design — so both deposits land.
A version column makes the lost update detectable instead of silent: the stale write matches 0 rows, and retrying against the new version lands both deposits — no locks held while the app thinks.
An INSERT on an idempotency key reports 1 affected row exactly once: the first request charges, every retry — even one racing the original in flight — gets 0 affected rows and charges nothing.

Every DDL statement performs an implicit COMMIT of the current transaction first: after a mid-transaction CREATE INDEX, the "uncommitted" work is permanently committed and a later ROLLBACK undoes nothing.
The full worker loop — claim with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, work, mark done, commit — never double-processes a job and never loses one: a worker crash returns its job to the queue automatically.

A UNIQUE constraint makes the concurrent duplicate wait for the first insert's fate and then fail with errno 1062 — and ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE turns that error into a clean upsert (INSERT IGNORE absorbs it, at a price).
Errno 1213 is transient, not fatal: the victim's transaction rerun from the top sees the survivor's committed state and succeeds — withRetry needs exactly two attempts here.
Two systems, two writes, no shared transaction: whichever write goes first, a failure between them leaves the database and the broker permanently disagreeing.

A saga replaces one distributed transaction with a chain of local ones: every step commits immediately and is visible to everyone, and a failed step is undone by a new compensating transaction — not by ROLLBACK.
Writing the order and its event in one transaction makes them atomic, and a SKIP LOCKED relay gives at-least-once delivery: a crashed relay redelivers the event instead of losing it.
XA PREPARE detaches a transaction from its session: it survives the session's death, keeps holding its locks, and any later session can finish it by name with XA COMMIT.
Every deadlock increments the server-wide lock_deadlocks counter in INNODB_METRICS — deadlocks are countable and alertable even if nobody saw the error, because the counter only ever goes up.

Two joins on information_schema.innodb_trx find the forgotten transaction: the oldest open transaction by trx_started, and the session that holds one open while doing nothing — including the read-only kind that never shows up in write metrics but still pins purge.
Two queries make undo bloat diagnosable: INNODB_METRICS' history list length says purge is falling behind, and a join on innodb_trx names the session whose old read view is holding it back.
max_execution_time cuts a runaway SELECT short without touching the session, and wait_timeout kills a connection that goes idle — rolling back whatever transaction it silently held open.
One query on sys.innodb_lock_waits names the waiter and the blocker, and a join to the processlist shows the blocker is sitting idle in transaction — and killing it drains the queue.

After division by zero in this explicit transaction, SELECT fails with 25P02; ROLLBACK ends the failed transaction and a new SELECT succeeds. In the second transaction, COMMIT after the error rolls back the preceding INSERT.
In this explicit transaction, a CHECK violation follows a successful credit; after ROLLBACK, both balances retain their original values.
B sees A's successful autocommit UPDATE in its next plain SELECT at READ COMMITTED; an explicit transaction's UPDATE becomes visible to B only after COMMIT.
In this schedule, CREATE TABLE and non-concurrent CREATE INDEX do not commit the preceding INSERT; after a statement error and ROLLBACK, the inserted row, new table, and new index are absent.
Rolling back to outer_sp removes the later rows and inner_sp; RELEASE outer_sp retains row 4, and COMMIT preserves rows 1 and 4.
ROLLBACK TO the savepoint recovers from this uniqueness violation; the earlier INSERT and a later replacement INSERT commit successfully.

At READ COMMITTED, both plain SELECTs read the original balance rather than the other transaction's uncommitted UPDATE; both writes later commit. This excludes a dirty-read cycle in this schedule, not every form of dependency cycle.

A's UPDATE at REPEATABLE READ fails with 40001 when B updates its target row after A's snapshot, both when B has already committed and when A waits for B to commit; when B rolls back instead, A's waiting UPDATE succeeds.
At READ COMMITTED, B's UPDATE of row 1 waits for A to commit before proceeding; after both transactions update both rows and commit in this order, both final prices are B's.
B's plain SELECT reads 100 while A's draft 999 is uncommitted, and its SELECT after A commits reads the final 110.
Two read-modify-write transactions at READ COMMITTED both read 100 and write 110; both commit, leaving 110 rather than the intended 120.
In this schedule at REPEATABLE READ, B's stale UPDATE fails with 40001 after A commits 110; after ROLLBACK, B reads 110 in a fresh transaction and commits 120.
B accepts the READ UNCOMMITTED setting but its plain SELECT reads the committed 100 rather than A's uncommitted 999, which A later rolls back.
A's plain SELECTs at READ COMMITTED return 100 and then 200 around B's committed UPDATE; in the following writer schedule, B waits for A's row lock before committing 400.
C's plain SELECTs at READ COMMITTED see both of A's committed balances while B's overwrites are uncommitted; after B commits both changes, C's next SELECT sees both of B's balances.
A's first aggregate at READ COMMITTED counts two matching orders; after B commits a matching INSERT, A's next aggregate counts three and totals 1500.

In this schedule, the REPEATABLE READ report commits with two receipts before the cashier commits a third into the closed batch; with all three transactions SERIALIZABLE, the report commits and the cashier's COMMIT fails with 40001.

At READ COMMITTED, A's separate SELECTs around B's committed transfer return balances totaling 125; in the second schedule at REPEATABLE READ, the two reads total 100 despite B's intervening transfer.

A's first plain SELECT at REPEATABLE READ includes B's change after BEGIN; subsequent SELECTs exclude B's later committed UPDATE and INSERT but include A's own UPDATE. After COMMIT, A's next SELECT sees all committed rows.
B's UPDATE at READ COMMITTED waits for A to commit, re-checks value = 10 against the changed row, and affects zero rows; the final values remain 20 and 30.
Both REPEATABLE READ transactions read two on-call doctors, update different rows, and commit in this schedule; the final asserted on-call count is zero.
With both transactions SERIALIZABLE, A commits and B's COMMIT fails with 40001 in this schedule; one doctor remains on call. B's fresh transaction observes one and leaves that doctor on call.

In this schedule ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN waits behind A's retained ACCESS SHARE, and C's new SELECT waits behind the queued ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request. Both complete after A commits; this is not a universal queue-order guarantee.
B's standalone ALTER waits for a lock and fails with 55P03 under a 100ms lock_timeout. C reads successfully after that request leaves the queue; B's retry after A commits adds the column.
In this two-row schedule both transfers lock rows in id order first. B waits for A, then both commit, leaving balances 115 and 85. Other resources and schedules are not tested.

In this opposite-order two-row schedule, with B's detection timeout shorter than A's, B gets 40P01, A completes and commits, and the asserted balances retain only A's transfer. General victim choice is not guaranteed.

In this immediate foreign-key insert schedule, B's non-key parent UPDATE succeeds, its DELETE waits for A, and after A commits the DELETE fails with 23503. This conflict signature is consistent with FOR KEY SHARE.

In this Read Committed schedule B's ordinary SELECT reads 100 while A holds FOR UPDATE; B's UPDATE waits, then uses A's committed 150 to leave 140. Locking reads can conflict; table-lock waits are not excluded.

This schedule asserts SHARE/SHARE coexistence, SHARE blocking a non-key UPDATE, KEY SHARE coexisting with that UPDATE, and FOR UPDATE waiting for it. The complete compatibility matrix is a manual contract.

In this single-row update schedule B completes after A commits while C remains waiting; after B commits C completes, and the balance is 211. This observation does not establish universal FIFO fairness.

B's standalone UPDATE fails with 55P03 under a 100ms lock_timeout while A holds the row lock. After A commits, B retries successfully and reads 300. lock_timeout limits each acquisition, not total statement time.

For this table and primary index, M asserts four pg_locks entries for A's UPDATE, B's ungranted transaction-id ShareLock, and B's direct blocker A. Ordinary on-disk row locks normally do not appear directly in pg_locks.

B's FOR UPDATE NOWAIT gets 55P03 while A holds a conflicting row lock; after A commits, B's standalone retry returns row 1. NOWAIT concerns row locks and does not eliminate table-lock waits or other errors.

In overlapping transactions, the scheduled FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED reads return jobs 1, 2 and 3, then no available row. After A explicitly rolls back, D reads job 1 again. No external execution or universal no-wait guarantee is established.

In this setup three updates leave four inspected tuple versions and one live value. Updating 1000 rows grows the heap from 5 to 9 pages; deleting them leaves zero live rows and 9 pages at the next observation. Reuse, pruning and vacuum can change later size.

With A holding an old Repeatable Read snapshot, VACUUM leaves the inspected jobs tuple-chain fields unchanged and A still reads new. After A commits, a second VACUUM reclaims the three obsolete versions. Other tables and other VACUUM work are not observed.

In this setup UPDATE creates a new tuple at (0,2), while B's old Repeatable Read snapshot still reads the original balance at (0,1). After DELETE there are zero live rows but both tuple versions remain in the inspected page. This is not a promise of permanent physical retention.

C's Repeatable Read snapshot records A as in progress and B as completed. C reads A's old value and B's committed value, repeats that view after A commits, then sees A's new value in a fresh transaction. The exposed snapshot components are not the complete tuple-visibility algorithm.

In this setup VACUUM frees inspected counters slots and the next INSERT reuses slot 2. Standard VACUUM leaves bloat at 9 pages; VACUUM FULL compacts it to 5. Standard VACUUM can truncate empty trailing pages under suitable locking conditions, a variant not executed here.

Advisory locks serialize application-defined work with no table involved: try-lock answers instantly, session-level locks survive COMMIT and need an explicit unlock, transaction-level locks vanish at COMMIT.
"SELECT first, INSERT if absent" cannot enforce uniqueness: two concurrent requests both see 0 rows, both insert, and the duplicate lands without any error.
UPDATE ... SET balance = balance + 10 reads and writes in one statement: the second writer waits for the first and stacks on top — both deposits survive.
When the new value must be computed in application code, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE serializes the read-modify-write: the second reader waits and then reads the committed 110, so both deposits land.
A version column makes the lost update detectable instead of silent: the stale write matches 0 rows (UPDATE 0), and retrying against the new version lands both deposits.

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING on an idempotency key makes retries safe: the first request charges, every retry — even one racing the original in flight — gets 0 rows back and charges nothing.

A session that goes idle mid-transaction (the classic ORM failure mode) is killed by idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: its work is rolled back and the app discovers the corpse on its next statement.
The full worker loop — claim with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, work, mark done, commit — never double-processes a job and never loses one: a worker crash returns its job to the queue automatically.
A UNIQUE constraint makes the concurrent duplicate wait for the first insert's fate and then fail with 23505 — and ON CONFLICT turns that error into a clean no-op or upsert.
A 40001 is transient, not fatal: rerunning the identical transaction reads the fresh state and succeeds — withRetry needs exactly two attempts here.
Two systems, two writes, no shared transaction: whichever write goes first, a failure between them leaves the database and the broker permanently disagreeing.
NOTIFY delivers nothing until COMMIT, a rolled-back NOTIFY is never delivered, and identical notifications within one transaction are folded into one.

A saga replaces one distributed transaction with a chain of local ones: every step commits immediately and is visible to everyone, and a failed step is undone by a new compensating transaction — not by ROLLBACK.
Writing the order and its event in one transaction makes them atomic, and a SKIP LOCKED relay gives at-least-once delivery: a crashed relay redelivers the event instead of losing it.

PREPARE TRANSACTION detaches a transaction from its session: it survives the session's death, keeps holding its locks, holds the xid horizon back so VACUUM reclaims nothing in any table, and any later session can finish it by name with COMMIT PREPARED.

A stuck worker's open transaction pins the vacuum horizon, so every claim/complete cycle the queue drains during the hang leaves a dead row version VACUUM cannot reclaim — the queue table grows with its throughput, not its backlog, and the identical VACUUM frees all of it the moment the worker's transaction ends.
Every deadlock increments pg_stat_database.deadlocks — a counter you can alert on even when nobody was watching the error logs.
Three pg_stat_activity queries find the forgotten transaction: the oldest xact_start, sessions sitting idle in transaction, and the backend_xmin that pins VACUUM's horizon.
statement_timeout cancels a runaway statement (SQLSTATE 57014) but keeps the session; transaction_timeout kills the whole transaction — connection and all — and its work rolls back.
pg_stat_user_tables shows dead tuples accumulating and when vacuum last ran, and age(datfrozenxid) vs autovacuum_freeze_max_age is the wraparound alert.
One join on pg_stat_activity + pg_blocking_pids() names the blocker, shows that it's sitting idle in transaction, and shows the last statement it ran — and pg_terminate_backend() drains the queue.
